title: Test a login form in 5 minutes
hook: Five checks that reveal common problems.

steps.label: Valid details
steps.detail: Can a real user sign in?

caption:
A login form looks simple—until you test more than the happy path. Start with valid credentials, an incorrect password, empty fields and password visibility. Then check recovery and how errors are displayed.

Which login bug have you encountered most often?

title: Write bug reports developers can use
hook: A useful report answers four questions.
takeaway: GOOD TITLE: 'Checkout fails after expired coupon'.
caption:
The goal of a bug report is not to sound technical. It's to make the issue easy to reproduce and understand.

Include environment, steps, actual result and expected result. Add a screenshot or short recording when it really helps.

Save this for your next testing session.

title: Smoke testing vs regression testing

steps.label: Smoke tests
steps.detail: Is this build stable enough to test?

takeaway: SCOPE depends on product risk and release changes.
caption:
Smoke testing is a quick check of critical functionality on a new build. Regression testing looks for unintended breakage in previously working behavior after changes.

They overlap sometimes, but their purpose and depth differ.

Which one does your team run more often?

title: A checklist beats a good memory

steps.label: Define the trigger
steps.detail: When should you use the list?

steps.label: Update after mistakes
steps.detail: Improve the list when you learn

takeaway: CHECKLISTS support judgment; they don't replace it.
caption:
A checklist is not proof that work is easy. It's a way to preserve attention for decisions instead of trying to remember repetitive steps.

Keep each item specific enough to verify, and revise the list when a new issue teaches you something.

title: Test the boundaries, not only the middle
hook: Input limits hide surprisingly useful bugs.

steps.label: Minimum
steps.detail: Try one character below the limit

caption:
Boundary value analysis is a simple way to prioritize tests around input limits.

If a name field accepts 3–20 characters, test 2, 3, 20 and 21—not just an ordinary 10-character value. Then consider whitespace, special characters and any normalization rules.

The specification is your source of truth.

title: Make spreadsheets easier to maintain
hook: A few rules save future-you time.

steps.label: One header row
steps.detail: Give every column a clear name

steps.label: Consistent statuses
steps.detail: Use a dropdown, not free text

steps.label: Separate raw and summary
steps.detail: Keep data entry distinct from totals

takeaway: LESS CLEANUP = more time for actual analysis.
caption:
A spreadsheet can be simple and still be well structured.

Use clear headers, controlled status options, a separate summary area, and avoid merging cells within the data table. These habits make sorting, filtering and formulas much more reliable.

What's your spreadsheet pet peeve?

title: A good reproduction step is specific
hook: Compare vague wording with a useful example.
takeaway: WRITE steps another person can repeat.
caption:
If someone else can't reproduce your bug, even a serious issue can become difficult to investigate.

Use numbered steps, exact inputs, the relevant environment and a clear observed outcome. Keep unrelated actions out of the sequence.

Good reproduction steps are a form of teamwork.

title: Don't forget form validation tests
hook: Four practical cases for almost any form.

steps.label: Empty required field
steps.detail: Is the user guided to fix it?

steps.label: Valid edge case
steps.detail: A value near an allowed limit

takeaway: VALIDATION should be checked on server too.
caption:
When checking a form, don't stop at whether the Submit button works. Test required fields, invalid formats, allowed boundary values and recovery after an error.

Client-side messages help users, but server-side validation remains important for enforcing rules.

title: Write notes your future self can use
hook: Context disappears faster than you think.

steps.label: Record the goal
steps.detail: What were you trying to achieve?

takeaway: NOTES should reduce re-discovery, not create noise.
caption:
A good technical note saves future-you a second investigation. Capture the goal, relevant environment, observed result and next action.

Even a short note can prevent an hour of trying to remember why something was changed.

title: What to check before a release
hook: Use this as a starting point, not a guarantee.

steps.label: Known issues
steps.detail: Open risks are visible to the team

steps.label: Monitoring & rollback
steps.detail: Know how to spot and undo trouble

takeaway: RELEASE decisions are about understood risk.
caption:
There is no checklist that guarantees a bug-free release. But a short, risk-based review can help your team make a better decision.

Check critical user journeys, outstanding defects, regression areas related to recent changes, and the plan for monitoring or rollback.

title: Track work with consistent statuses

steps.label: Blocked
steps.detail: Cannot execute due to a dependency

takeaway: KEEP status definitions written down and consistent.
caption:
If one tester writes 'Done', another writes 'OK' and a third writes 'Passed', your dashboard starts lying.

Agree on a small set of statuses and what they mean. Dropdowns help keep the data consistent—whether you're tracking tests, tasks or reviews.

title: Turn acceptance criteria into tests
hook: A simple Given / When / Then example.

steps.label: Given
steps.detail: A signed-in user has items in cart

steps.label: When
steps.detail: They apply a valid discount code

takeaway: CRITERIA describe behavior; tests probe it.
caption:
Acceptance criteria describe expected behavior. Test cases make it observable—and often reveal missing scenarios.

For a discount feature, start with a valid code, then examine expired, invalid or already-used codes as the rules require.

Good questions during refinement prevent confusion later.
